title: Unescaped HTML sink {sink} ({lang}) — review required
description: The {lang} sink {sink} writes a value into HTML without escaping. If the value contains untrusted input, attacker markup and scripts run in victims' browsers. This lexical rule flags the sink; the reviewer confirms the value is trusted or escaped.
remediation: Escape the value for its HTML context ({safe}) or bind it as text, never markup. Only trusted constant markup may bypass escaping.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: any {sink} call matches, including trusted constant markup. Whether the value is attacker-controlled needs human review.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on the {sink} call in {lang} code.
fp: Rendering trusted constant templates is the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} inserts raw markup into a page. Unescaped sinks turn stored or reflected input into script execution in the victim's session. The {lang}-specific remedy is contextual escaping via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} codebases rendering values through {sink}; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Stored or reflected cross-site scripting when untrusted input reaches the sink; MEDIUM severity, HIGH for stored sinks on authenticated pages.
why: {sink} writes unescaped markup in {lang}, so untrusted input reaching it becomes cross-site scripting.
fix: Escape the value with {safe} or bind it as text content.
If raw markup is required, sanitize it against an allowlist of tags and attributes.
Re-run the scan and confirm no {sink} call remains reachable from untrusted input.
verifyT: Rescan shows no {sink} reachable from untrusted input, and markup probes render inert.

title: Raw-markup binding ({lang}: {sink}) — review required
description: A {lang} template or component binds a value as raw markup: {sink}. Untrusted input in the value runs as script in victims' browsers. This lexical rule flags the binding; the reviewer confirms the value is trusted or switches to text binding.
remediation: Bind the value as text ({safe}) or sanitize it against a tag allowlist before raw binding.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the binding regardless of value trust. Call-shaped sinks are separate rules.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on the raw-markup binding in {lang} templates or code.
fp: Trusted constant markup bound for layout is the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} disables the framework's automatic escaping for one binding. Raw-markup bindings exist for trusted rich text, but any untrusted bytes in the value become script. The remedy is text binding via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} templates and components using the raw binding; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Cross-site scripting, usually stored; MEDIUM severity, HIGH on authenticated pages.
why: {sink} binds unescaped markup in {lang}, so untrusted input in the value becomes script execution.
fix: Replace the raw binding with {safe}.
If raw markup is required, sanitize the value against an allowlist first.
Re-run the scan and confirm no raw binding remains reachable from untrusted input.
verifyT: Rescan shows no raw binding reachable from untrusted input, and markup probes render inert.

cweDef.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')
cweDef.summary: User input reaches a file path without confinement, so ../ sequences escape the intended directory.

title: File access built from input ({lang}) — review required
description: A {lang} file operation builds its path from concatenated or interpolated input: {sink}. Directory-traversal sequences in the input escape the intended directory. This lexical rule flags the construction; the reviewer confirms the input is confined or mapped through an allowlist.
remediation: Resolve the path against a base directory with {safe} and reject results outside it, or map input through an allowlist of file ids.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: any concatenated path matches, including trusted ones. Whether the input is attacker-controlled needs human review.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on input-built file paths in {lang} code.
fp: Joining trusted configuration directories is the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} assembles a filesystem path from parts. Traversal payloads (..%2f, absolute paths, symlink races) redirect the operation outside its directory. The {lang}-specific remedy is confinement via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} codebases opening files with assembled paths; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Arbitrary file read or write when untrusted input reaches the path; HIGH severity because traversal payloads are trivial and impact is filesystem-wide.
why: {lang} file access assembles paths from input ({sink}), so traversal sequences escape the intended directory.
fix: Confine the resolved path under its base directory with {safe} and reject escapes.
Prefer an allowlist mapping opaque input ids to fixed paths.
Re-run the scan and confirm no assembled path remains reachable from untrusted input.
verifyT: Rescan shows no assembled path reachable from untrusted input, and traversal probes are rejected.

title: Archive extraction via {sink} ({lang}) — review required
description: The {lang} call {sink} extracts archive entries to disk. A hostile archive can carry traversal entry names (../../) that write outside the target directory. This lexical rule flags the extraction; the reviewer confirms entry names are validated or confined.
remediation: Validate every entry name with {safe} before writing, rejecting absolute paths and parent traversal.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: any {sink} call matches, including extraction of trusted archives. Archive trust needs human review.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on the {sink} call in {lang} code.
fp: Extracting bundled, trusted archives is the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} writes archive members to the filesystem. Entry names are attacker-controlled metadata in hostile archives, so extraction without name checks is a write primitive. The remedy is per-entry validation via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} codebases extracting archives through {sink}; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Arbitrary file overwrite (Zip Slip) from hostile archives; HIGH severity because archives routinely cross trust boundaries.
why: {sink} extracts {lang} archives without name checks, so traversal entries write outside the target directory.
fix: Check every entry name with {safe}, rejecting absolute paths, .. segments, and symlinks.
Extract into an empty directory and verify its contents before use.
Re-run the scan and confirm extraction is guarded.
verifyT: Rescan shows extraction guarded, and a traversal-entry archive writes nothing outside its directory.

cweDef.name: Insecure Temporary File
cweDef.summary: Temporary files use predictable names or weak creation, letting attackers pre-create or swap them.

title: Insecure temporary file via {sink} ({lang}) — review required
description: The {lang} call {sink} creates temporary files with predictable names or unsafe semantics, so a local attacker can pre-create or replace the file (symlink attacks). This lexical rule flags the call; the reviewer confirms exclusive creation or switches to {safe}.
remediation: Create temporary files with {safe}, which opens exclusively with tight permissions.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: any {sink} call matches regardless of directory protections.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on the {sink} call in {lang} code.
fp: Single-user scripts in protected directories are the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} names temporary files predictably or separates name choice from creation, opening a race window. The remedy is atomic exclusive creation via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} codebases creating temporary files through {sink}; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Local file overwrite or disclosure via symlink races; LOW severity, higher on multi-user systems.
why: {sink} creates {lang} temporary files insecurely, so local attackers can intercept them.
fix: Replace {sink} with {safe}.
Set tight permissions on any file that must persist.
Re-run the scan and confirm no insecure creation remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no {sink}, and temporary files are created exclusively.

title: Overly broad file permissions ({lang}) — review required
description: Code in {lang} grants world-writable or world-readable permissions: {sink}. Any local user can then modify or read the file. This lexical rule flags the grant; the reviewer confirms the breadth is intended or tightens it.
remediation: Grant the narrowest workable mode ({safe}) and rely on group ownership instead of world bits.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the mode regardless of file sensitivity.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on broad permission grants in {lang} code or scripts.
fp: Intentionally public data files are the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} sets permission bits that include world access. Broad modes on code, keys, or data turn any local account into a writer or reader. The remedy is least-privilege modes via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} code and scripts setting file modes; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Local tampering or disclosure; MEDIUM severity, HIGH for executables, keys, and configuration.
why: {lang} code grants world access ({sink}), so any local user can read or modify the file.
fix: Replace the mode with {safe}.
Use group ownership for sharing instead of world bits.
Re-run the scan and confirm no broad grant remains on sensitive files.
verifyT: Rescan shows no broad grant, and file modes audit tight.

cweDef.name: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect')
cweDef.summary: Redirect targets take untrusted input, so phishing links abuse the site's domain for credibility.

title: Redirect via {sink} ({lang}) — review required
description: The {lang} call {sink} redirects the user to a computed address. If the address derives from untrusted input, phishing links gain the site's credibility. This lexical rule flags the call; the reviewer confirms the target is fixed or validated.
remediation: Redirect only to fixed paths or validate the target with {safe} before redirecting.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: any {sink} call matches, including fixed-target redirects.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on the {sink} call in {lang} code.
fp: Fixed post-login landing pages are the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} issues a redirect to a caller-chosen address. Open targets let attackers craft trusted-looking links to hostile sites. The remedy is target validation via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} request handlers redirecting through {sink}; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Phishing and token theft via trusted-domain links; MEDIUM severity, HIGH when redirects carry tokens.
why: {sink} redirects {lang} users to a computed address, so untrusted input in the target enables phishing.
fix: Validate the target with {safe}, allowing only relative paths or listed hosts.
Drop untrusted redirect parameters in favor of fixed destinations.
Re-run the scan and confirm no open target remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no open redirect, and hostile targets are rejected.

apex: a fixed allowlist of page names

title: SQL built by concatenation ({lang}) — review required
description: A {lang} query call assembles SQL from parts: {sink}. If any part is untrusted input, the query structure itself is attacker-controlled. This lexical rule flags the assembly; the reviewer confirms every part is trusted or parameterizes it.
remediation: Parameterize with {safe} so input stays data; never interpolate values into SQL text.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: any concatenated query matches, including trusted assembly. Input trust needs human review.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on concatenated SQL in {lang} code.
fp: Assembling fixed column lists or trusted fragments is the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} mixes code and data in one SQL string. Concatenation is the classic injection primitive: quotes and keywords in the input rewrite the statement. The remedy is bound parameters via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} codebases issuing SQL through the flagged call; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Full database compromise (read, write, execute) when untrusted input reaches the query; HIGH severity.
why: {lang} SQL is assembled from parts ({sink}), so untrusted input rewrites the statement.
fix: Rewrite the query with {safe}, binding every value as a parameter.
For dynamic identifiers, map input through an allowlist of columns and tables.
Re-run the scan and confirm no concatenated query remains on untrusted input.
verifyT: Rescan shows no concatenated query on untrusted input, and quote payloads stay inert data.

cweDef.name: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')
cweDef.summary: Untrusted input reaches code generation, so template or expression text becomes executable.

title: Template compiled from input ({lang}) — review required
description: A {lang} template engine compiles a template built from parts: {sink}. Template syntax in the input executes with the application's authority. This lexical rule flags the compilation; the reviewer confirms the template is fixed or sandboxed.
remediation: Compile fixed templates only and pass input as variables ({safe}); never build template source from input.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: any assembled template matches, including trusted ones.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on assembled templates in {lang} code.
fp: Assembling fixed template names (not source) is the common false positive — confirm which is assembled.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} turns a string into an executable template. Server-side template injection runs attacker expressions with application data access. The remedy is fixed templates with variable binding via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} codebases compiling templates from assembled strings; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Server-side template injection leading to data theft or code execution; HIGH severity.
why: {lang} templates compile from assembled source ({sink}), so input syntax executes with application authority.
fix: Use fixed template files with {safe} variable binding.
If dynamic templates are required, sandbox them without sensitive context.
Re-run the scan and confirm no assembled template source remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no assembled template source, and expression probes render inert.

cweDef.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an LDAP Query ('LDAP Injection')
cweDef.summary: Untrusted input reaches LDAP filters, so metacharacters rewrite the directory query.

title: LDAP filter built by concatenation ({lang}) — review required
description: A {lang} directory call assembles an LDAP filter from parts: {sink}. Filter metacharacters in untrusted input rewrite the query, bypassing authentication or dumping entries. This lexical rule flags the assembly; the reviewer confirms escaping or parameterization.
remediation: Escape filter values with {safe} or use parameterized directory APIs.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: any assembled filter matches, including trusted ones.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on assembled LDAP filters in {lang} code.
fp: Assembling fixed organizational units is the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} mixes filter syntax with values. LDAP metacharacters (*, (, ), \) in input alter which entries match. The remedy is value escaping via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} codebases querying directories with assembled filters; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Authentication bypass and directory disclosure; HIGH severity for login paths.
why: {lang} LDAP filters assemble from parts ({sink}), so input metacharacters rewrite the query.
fix: Escape every value with {safe} before interpolation.
Prefer parameterized directory calls where the library offers them.
Re-run the scan and confirm no raw interpolation remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no raw filter interpolation, and metacharacter input matches literally.

cweDef.name: XML Injection (aka Blind XPath Injection)
cweDef.summary: Untrusted input reaches XPath or XML construction, so query syntax escapes its intended bounds.

title: XPath built by concatenation ({lang}) — review required
description: A {lang} XML call assembles an XPath from parts: {sink}. Quote-breaking input rewrites the query and reads unintended nodes. This lexical rule flags the assembly; the reviewer confirms quoting or variable binding.
remediation: Bind values as XPath variables ({safe}) instead of interpolating them.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: any assembled XPath matches, including trusted ones.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on assembled XPath in {lang} code.
fp: Assembling fixed element paths is the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} embeds values in XPath text. Quote and axis syntax in input escapes the intended predicate. The remedy is variable binding via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} codebases querying XML with assembled paths; single-line lexical scope.
risk: XML disclosure and authentication bypass on XPath-based checks; HIGH severity.
why: {lang} XPath assembles from parts ({sink}), so input quotes rewrite the query.
fix: Bind values as variables with {safe}.
If binding is unavailable, quote-escape values before interpolation.
Re-run the scan and confirm no raw interpolation remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no raw XPath interpolation, and quote payloads match literally.

cweDef.name: Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences in HTTP Headers ('HTTP Request/Response Splitting')
cweDef.summary: CR or LF reaches a header value, splitting one response into attacker-controlled headers or bodies.

title: Response header built from input ({lang}) — review required
description: A {lang} response call sets a header from assembled parts: {sink}. CRLF sequences in untrusted input split the response and inject headers or body bytes. This lexical rule flags the assembly; the reviewer confirms the value is validated.
remediation: Validate the value against {safe} (no CR/LF, expected charset) before setting the header.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: any assembled header matches; modern frameworks often reject CRLF, which the reviewer should confirm.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on assembled response headers in {lang} code.
fp: Frameworks that reject CRLF in header values make many hits non-exploitable — confirm the behavior.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} places a computed value in a response header. CR and LF bytes end the header early, letting the remainder become new headers or body. The remedy is strict value validation ({safe}).
applicability: {lang} response paths setting headers from parts; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Response splitting: header injection, cache poisoning, script injection; MEDIUM severity (frameworks mitigate).
why: {lang} response headers assemble from parts ({sink}), so CRLF in input splits the response.
fix: Validate the value with {safe}, rejecting CR, LF, and unexpected bytes.
Prefer framework header APIs that encode or reject control bytes.
Re-run the scan and confirm no raw header assembly remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no raw header assembly, and CRLF probes are rejected.
